planting.note: Set out container-grown offsets in spring once nights stay above freezing, in fast-draining mineral soil; in containers use a heavy pumice or grit mix and bring indoors well before the first hard frost in marginal climates.

directions: Native to the dry hillsides of Oaxaca and Puebla, Mexico, Black-spined Agave forms a dense, symmetrical rosette of narrow, glaucous blue-gray leaves tipped with a long, glossy black terminal spine and fine black marginal teeth. It clusters readily from basal offsets over time, forming attractive multi-headed clumps in rock gardens and containers. Plant in full sun in lean, sharply drained soil and water only when the root zone has dried completely, since rot from winter wet is a far greater risk than cold. It is slow-growing and monocarpic, flowering only once after many years on a tall stalk before the rosette that bloomed dies back.

planting.note: Divide and transplant rooted offsets in spring into gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun; this species tolerates more cold and some winter moisture than most agaves but still prefers a raised or sloped planting site.

directions: Striped Agave forms an unusual ball-shaped rosette of hundreds of slender, needle-like leaves, each striped in bands of green, red, and cream that intensify in strong sun and cold. Native to the Chihuahuan Desert of Coahuila and Nuevo Leon, it offsets freely at the base to build a dense, textural clump that reads almost like a pincushion in the landscape. It is notably more cold-tolerant than many agave species and is a good choice for rock gardens and xeriscapes in climates with occasional hard freezes, provided drainage is excellent. Grow in full sun in lean, rocky soil and water sparingly, letting the soil dry fully between waterings.

planting.note: Plant small nursery-grown offsets in spring in a shallow, extremely well-drained grit or scree mix in full to part sun; this rare, tiny species resents any standing moisture and does best in containers or raised rock crevices.

directions: Widely regarded as the smallest agave species, this dwarf rarity forms a rosette only a few inches across of dark green leaves marked with crisp white bud-print patterning and fine curling white filaments along the margins. It is native to rocky grassland slopes of southern Arizona and adjacent Sonora, where it grows tucked among grasses and shrubs for partial protection. Because of its tiny size it is very slow to mature and highly sensitive to overwatering and crown rot, so it is best grown in a shallow pot or raised scree bed with maximum drainage. Give full sun on the coast or in high-elevation sites, but light afternoon shade in hot, low-desert gardens.

planting.note: Set out rooted offsets in spring in a gritty, mineral-rich potting mix or raised bed in full sun; this compact species is widely grown in containers and should be sheltered from prolonged winter wet.

directions: Isthmus Agave is a compact, dwarf species from the Isthmus of Tehuantepec region of Oaxaca, closely allied to Agave potatorum but distinguished by its smaller, broader, more cupped gray-green leaves and shorter, reddish-brown terminal spines. It forms a tidy, symmetrical rosette rarely exceeding a foot across, making it one of the most popular small agaves for pots and tight garden spaces, and it is the parent of several well-known variegated nursery selections. Grow in full sun in fast-draining, lean soil, and water only when the root zone is fully dry, since it is considerably less cold-tolerant than larger desert agave species. Protect from hard freezes and prolonged winter rain to prevent rot.

planting.note: Plant rooted bulbils or basal offsets in spring in well-drained desert soil in full sun; established clumps need little supplemental water once settled in beyond occasional deep irrigation.

directions: Murphey's Agave forms a broad, open rosette of smooth gray-green leaves and holds particular historical significance as a species widely propagated and dispersed by the Hohokam people of central Arizona, who cultivated it near prehistoric agricultural sites for food and fiber. It reproduces chiefly through bulbils produced on its flower stalk and through basal offsets rather than seed, since it flowers only rarely in cultivation. Plant in full sun in rocky, fast-draining desert soil, where it is notably drought-tolerant once established and needs only occasional deep watering during the hottest months. It is a good mid-sized architectural accent for xeriscape beds and is more cold-hardy than many Mexican agave species.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring in rocky, well-drained soil in full sun; this sky-island native establishes slowly and benefits from a raised planting site in heavier garden soils.

directions: Mountain Yucca is a tree-form species native to oak-pine canyons of the sky-island ranges of southeastern Arizona, southwestern New Mexico, and northern Mexico, where it grows at higher, cooler elevations than most tree yuccas. It develops broad, smooth-edged blue-green leaves without the curling marginal fibers typical of many yuccas, and over decades forms a stout single or branching trunk topped by dense leaf heads. In early summer it produces large, showy panicles of cream-white, often purple-tinged flowers well above the foliage. Plant in full sun in rocky, sharply drained soil; it is markedly more cold-hardy than lowland desert yuccas and tolerates occasional snow and hard freezes once established.
